title: New Founder Archetypes in the AI Age | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: Andrew Chen of a16z speedrun argues AI is widening the set of viable founder profiles (solo, non-technical, domain-expert, young, creator) and that investor 'yes/no' archetype rules are partly artifacts of each era's technology, distribution and self-reinforcing consensus funding. He cautions against replacing old pattern-matching with new slogans, since durable skills like sales, recruiting, judgment and persistence do not get easier.

insights.claim: AI may let one founder do what once took two or three cofounders (business, technical, GTM), but the counter-case is that a team multiplied by AI leverage still out-progresses a solo founder with the same leverage, and that seed-stage v1 expectations simply rise.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Do not underwrite 'solo founder' as a category edge; the bar for seed-stage v1 may rise in step with tooling.
insights.quote: On the other hand, Ben’s point is that maybe the v1 of a product, or what’s expected as a seed-stage startup just goes up.

insights.claim: Coding may never have been the main bottleneck for startups; agentic coding does not remove the need for many customer meetings, so solo founders may remain constrained on go-to-market.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Leverage in code production does not translate one-for-one into company-building speed; sales and customer discovery remain human-time bound.
insights.quote: Maybe coding was never the main bottleneck for startups in the first place?

insights.claim: A solo founder might do the work of ten people, but a team of three might do the work of thirty, so team size retains a multiplicative advantage under AI.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Favors small AI-native teams over solos when sizing conviction on founding configurations.
insights.quote: A solo founder might be able to do the work of ten people, but a team of three might be able to do the work of thirty.

insights.claim: AI lets elite non-technical talent from finance, consulting and creative industries build products themselves, but the gap between a demo and a reliable, scalable product persists, so technical judgment on what to build and what is possible may become more valuable as first versions commoditize.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Expect a flood of prototypes; durable differentiation shifts toward technical judgment, especially in dev tools.
insights.quote: maybe technical judgment becomes more important in deciding what to build, what’s actually possible

insights.claim: Domain experts (doctors, brokers, teachers, soldiers) can now use software to solve their own problems, but outsiders have historically reinvented industries: hoteliers did not create Airbnb and the finance industry did not create Kalshi.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Domain depth helps find problems but may impair first-principles rethinking; incumbents-turned-founders likely yield incremental products.
insights.quote: Hoteliers didn’t create Airbnb and the finance industry didn’t create Kalshi.

insights.claim: Domain expertise may help founders find problems yet make it harder to rethink an industry from scratch, e.g. dentists building AI dentist software have experience but may lack a disruptive outsider mindset.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Vertical AI built by practitioners may skew incremental; weigh against outsider-led entrants.
insights.quote: Domain expertise might help you find problems but make it harder to rethink an industry from scratch.

insights.claim: Young people who start with Minecraft mods, Roblox games and Discord bots already ship products used by thousands; AI lets them build more, earlier, though building what friends love differs from running a company (hiring, fundraising, monetization).
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Youth edge likely concentrated in consumer; limited in enterprise, healthcare and other relationship-heavy sectors.
insights.quote: Building something your friends love is very different from building a company.

insights.claim: Content creators bring built-in distribution and audience insight and can now ship software without a technical cofounder, but follower spikes are not a sustainable growth engine, since the most valuable products are long-running and endlessly iterated rather than memes.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Creator-led launches may show strong early metrics that overstate durability; diligence on retention and iteration capacity.
insights.quote: Having followers helps with a spike of distribution, but building a sustainable growth engine is something else.

insights.claim: Each startup wave minted a favored founder archetype: Stanford PhDs after Google, dropouts building Web 2.0 social apps for friends at Facebook, designery hipsters building mobile experiences at Airbnb, and gritty operational founders building on-demand apps at Uber, with computer science PhDs possibly returning in the AI infra age.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Archetype preference is cyclical and tied to the era; AI infra may re-elevate technical PhDs while application layer opens to others.
insights.quote: Each startup wave produces a new highly desirable archetype that gets hot, until the next one hits

insights.claim: Conventional investor 'no' rules include avoiding solo founders, non-technical founders, hoteliers building tech, dentists, content creators and celebrities, and being skeptical of international founders and married couples; the author argues AI may invalidate some of these.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Pattern-matching filters used by seed investors are a potential source of mispricing if AI shifts which profiles can succeed.
insights.quote: But what if some of these end up being all wrong?

insights.claim: Founder archetypes succeed because they fit the era's technology and distribution channels: viral email invites favored college students with .edu emails, App Store editorial picks favored well-connected designery developers, and iPhone GPS unlocked on-demand.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: When distribution channels shift (e.g., toward AI-native distribution), the winning founder profile should shift with them.
insights.quote: each founders’ opportunity is unlocked by the underlying technology cycle and distribution channels

insights.claim: Investor consensus on what a founder should look like creates a self-reinforcing loop: each investment of that type is safer and attracts more capital, and founders may get multiple 'unfair' rounds even when things are not working.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Consensus archetypes can carry inflated valuations and funding persistence; off-archetype founders may be underpriced.
insights.quote: the founder may have multiple “unfair” rounds given to them even when things aren’t quite working out

insights.claim: The self-reinforcing archetype effect matters most at pre-seed and seed, where rounds are fragmented and many investors must say yes for small checks to assemble.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Social proof and herd behavior dominate early-stage capital formation, creating an edge for investors willing to lead off-pattern.
insights.quote: where rounds are often fragmented where many people have to say yes for a bunch of small checks to come together

insights.claim: The author expects a rapid expansion in the types of founders building products, with high failure rates but some successes, and views a bigger tent as positive.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Expect broader founder demographics and higher variance in early-stage deal flow.
insights.quote: I think we’ll most certainly see a rapid expansion in the types of founder archetypes building new products.

insights.claim: The key question is which old founder assumptions were fundamental versus artifacts of past technology and distribution; coding gets easier while sales, recruiting, judgment and persistence do not, and some rules will almost certainly disappear.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Separate durable founder traits (sales, recruiting, judgment, persistence) from era-specific ones when screening.
insights.quote: Coding might get easier while sales, recruiting, judgment, and persistence don’t.

insights.claim: The mistake would be replacing old pattern matching with a new version such as 'solo founders are good now', since the profiles that work should change as the underlying technology changes.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Avoid swapping one archetype heuristic for another; evaluate individual-to-moment fit.
insights.quote: The mistake would be to replace the old pattern matching with a new version

insights.claim: a16z speedrun writes first checks of up to $1M into brand-new startups and runs an SF residency whose application deadline was November 1st.
insights.speaker: Andrew Chen
insights.so_what: Shows a16z's early-stage vehicle is actively recruiting nontraditional founder profiles.
insights.quote: where we write the first check into brand new startups (up to $1M)
